title: Three Input Layers: Designing for Phone, Headset, and AR Glasses Simultaneously
author: Patrouch & ZCode
excerpt: AmbientX now has three coexisting input systems: DOM buttons for flat screens, VR controller grip-throw for headsets, and a touchless hand-gesture pointer using MediaPipe for future AR glasses. The platform determines which layer is primary — no platform detection needed.

sections.title: Patrouch:
sections.content: Controlling the avatar VRM with MediaPipe is more compelling than using a joystick or WASD, for the most part. But now I've complicated things by adding VRM avatars as audience members who can lance tomatoes with a physical arm throw. What might be even more compelling is the ability to view the theater from inside the avatar. How to go back and forth?

sections.title: ZCode:
sections.content: The key move is separating locomotion and embodiment — they're already different systems. Arms and torso stay 1:1 body-tracked for the throw mechanics, while a separate locomotion layer handles translation through the theater. That's how every social VR app handles full-body tracking, because your physical play space will never be as big as a theater.

sections.title: Patrouch:
sections.content: Great answers, and probably completely logical given the VR context, but my WebXR isn't just about VR; I've tried to build it so that it can be useful without goggles.

sections.title: ZCode:
sections.content: That reframes everything. Third-person cameras are the default on flat screens — free-orbit, smooth transitions, cinematic cuts, nothing needs comfort engineering the way it does in VR. On desktop/mobile, first person vs third person is just a camera preference. The free-cam ghost mode that's risky for VR is just a normal camera toggle on flat screen.

sections.title: Patrouch:
sections.content: So what about touchless control interfaces? What about Meta Connect 2026 — AR glasses with displays?

sections.title: ZCode:
sections.content:
We built three input layers that coexist. The platform determines which one the user reaches for:

**Flat screen (phone/desktop):** DOM bottom bar buttons + drag-to-throw + touchless hand pointer. The bar auto-hides after 5 seconds. Drag anywhere to fling a tomato.

**VR headset (Quest):** In-world 3D menu panel floating in the theater, interacted with via controller ray or hand pinch. VR controller grip-swing-release throws tomatoes with real velocity computed from a 5-frame position buffer.

**AR glasses (future):** In-world 3D panel + touchless hand pointer. Your index finger becomes the cursor, pinch to click. No controller needed.

The touchless pointer reuses the existing MediaPipe HolisticLandmarker's rightHandLandmarks — index finger tip (landmark 8) maps to screen position, thumb-index pinch distance triggers a click. No separate model, no extra compute cost. It dispatches a real DOM click via document.elementFromPoint, so existing buttons receive it naturally.

sections.title: Patrouch:
sections.content: So if we had Meta glasses, say the Ray-Bans, we could use the in-world menu and not the bottom bar?

sections.title: ZCode:
sections.content: The current Ray-Ban Metas can't show a 3D menu — they have no display layer. They're camera + audio only. But the in-world panel is ready and waiting for any device that CAN render 3D. When AR glasses with actual displays arrive, the 3D panel will be the natural interaction method — you'd look at the floating panel in your living room and tap it with your finger. The DOM bottom bar is the reliable fallback for everything else, and that's not a compromise — it's the right UX for flat screens.

sections.title: Patrouch:
sections.content: Keep writing clean, modular ECS code where your Transform components serve as the absolute source of truth. Make sure your experiences are designed to layer neatly on top of a user's real living room rather than demanding they blindfold themselves with a plastic visor.
